sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale et complete produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo57/1g.xml (Perseus Digital Library, d'apres l'edition Oxford Classical Text de E.C. Marchant, 1921), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Le decoupage en 21 chapitres et en sections numerotees suit exactement la structure TEI de la source (397 sections au total ; chaque section source correspond a un paragraphe de cette traduction). Les titres de chapitres sont fournis par le traducteur pour la lisibilite, le texte grec n'en comportant pas. Il s'agit d'un dialogue socratique sur la gestion du domaine et de la maisonnee : les chapitres 1-2 opposent Socrate et Critobule sur la nature de la richesse ; a partir du chapitre 6, Socrate rapporte un long entretien avec Ischomaque, gentleman-modele (kalos kagathos), sur la formation de sa jeune epouse et la conduite de son domaine, de sa maisonnee et de ses cultures - y compris la longue comparaison de la maisonnee a une ruche et a sa reine (7.32-7.39), conservee integralement comme centrale a l'argument de l'oeuvre, et non ecartee comme bruit d'apparat (a la difference des notices factuelles sans rapport trouvees dans d'autres textes de ce corpus).

div.head: What is wealth? The definition of household management
div.p: I once heard him discoursing on household management too, in this manner. Tell me, Critobulus, he said, is household management the name of some branch of knowledge, just as medicine, metalworking, and carpentry are? It seems so to me, said Critobulus.

And just as we could name the function of each of these arts, could we likewise say what the function of household management is? It seems, at any rate, said Critobulus, to be the function of a good household manager to manage his own household well.

And could not a man, said Socrates, if entrusted with another's household, manage it well too, if he wished, just as he manages his own? For one who understands carpentry could work equally well for another as for himself, and so surely could the good household manager. It seems so to me, Socrates.

It is possible, then, said Socrates, for a man who understands this art, even if he himself happens to have no property, to earn wages managing another's household, just as he might building a house? Yes, by Zeus, said Critobulus, and he would earn a good wage too, if, taking over a household, he could pay all that is owed and, by creating a surplus, increase the household.

Now what do we think a household is? Is it the same as a house, or is everything a man possesses outside his house also part of his household? It seems to me, said Critobulus, that everything a man possesses is part of his household, even if it is not in the same city as the owner.

Well then, do some men also possess enemies? Yes indeed, some possess many. Shall we then say their enemies too are their possessions? It would be ridiculous, said Critobulus, if a man who increases his enemies' wealth should also be paid a wage for doing so!

For it seemed to us that a man's household was the same as his property. Yes, by Zeus, said Critobulus, whatever is good that a man possesses; but if it is something bad, I do not call that property. You seem to be calling property only what is useful to each. Certainly, he said; but what is harmful I count rather a loss than wealth.

So if a man buys a horse and does not know how to use it, but is thrown and injured by it, is the horse not property to him? No, if indeed property must be something good. Then neither is land property to a man who works it in such a way that he is harmed by his labour. Nor is land property either, if instead of feeding him it makes him hungry.

And likewise sheep too: if a man is harmed through not knowing how to make use of sheep, would the sheep not be property to him either? It seems not to me. You, it appears, count as wealth what benefits, but not what harms. Exactly so.

The very same things, then, are wealth to the man who knows how to use each of them, but not wealth to the man who does not know how: just as pipes are wealth to a man who understands how to play them well, but to a man who does not, they are worth no more than useless stones -- unless indeed he should sell them.

This, then, appears to us: pipes are wealth if sold, but not wealth if kept and not sold, by one who does not know how to use them. And our argument, Socrates, proceeds consistently, since we have said that what benefits is wealth. For unsold, the pipes are not wealth, since they are of no use; sold, they become wealth.

To this Socrates replied: Yes, if indeed he knows how to sell. But if he should sell them again for something he does not know how to use, the pipes, even when sold, are not wealth, by your own argument. You seem to mean, Socrates, that not even silver is wealth, unless a man knows how to use it.

And you too seem to agree with this, that whatever a man can be benefited by is wealth. Suppose, for instance, a man should use his silver to buy, say, a mistress, and through her his body were made worse, his soul worse, and his household worse -- how could the silver still be a benefit to him? In no way, unless we are to say that henbane too is wealth, by eating which men go mad.

Let silver, then, Critobulus, if a man does not know how to use it, be cast off so far that it is not even reckoned as wealth. But friends -- if a man knows how to use them so as to be benefited by them -- what shall we say they are? Wealth, by Zeus, said Critobulus, and far more so than cattle, if indeed they prove more beneficial than cattle.

Then enemies too, by your argument, are wealth to the man able to derive benefit from his enemies. So it seems to me at least. It is, then, the business of a good household manager to know how to use even his enemies so as to be benefited by them. Most certainly. And indeed, Critobulus, you see how many private households have been increased by war, and how many by tyranny.

Well, Socrates, said Critobulus, what you say seems to me finely put; but what shall we make of this: when we see men who possess the knowledge and the means by which, by working, they could increase their households, and yet we perceive they are unwilling to do so, and on this account we see their knowledge doing them no good -- is it not the case that for these men neither their knowledge nor their possessions are wealth after all?

Are you attempting, Critobulus, said Socrates, to discuss slaves? No, by Zeus, not I, but men held to be of quite excellent birth, some of whom I observe possessing skills of war, others skills of peace, yet unwilling to put these to work -- because, I think, they have no masters over them.

And how, said Socrates, could they have no masters, if, though praying to be happy and wishing to do the things from which they might gain good things, they are then hindered from doing these very things by their rulers? And who, said Critobulus, are these rulers, who, being invisible, rule over them?

But by Zeus, said Socrates, they are not invisible at all -- they are quite plainly visible. And that they are the basest of rulers does not escape you either, if indeed you consider idleness, softness of soul, and negligence to be baseness.

And there are other deceitful mistresses too, who pass themselves off as pleasures -- dicing and useless company with men -- who, as time goes on, become plain even to those they have deceived to be pains disguised in the wrapping of pleasures, since, gaining mastery, they hinder men from beneficial work.

But others, Socrates, said he, are not hindered from working by these; indeed they are very eager to work and to contrive revenues, yet nonetheless they wear down their households and are caught up in helplessness.

For these too are slaves, said Socrates, and to very harsh masters indeed: some to gluttony, some to lechery, some to drunkenness, and some to foolish and costly ambitions, which rule so harshly over the men they master that, so long as they see them still young and able to work, they compel them to bring whatever they earn and spend it upon their own desires; but when they perceive them unable to work any longer on account of old age, they abandon them to a wretched old age, and try instead to make use of other slaves.

But it is necessary, Critobulus, to fight against these no less hard for one's freedom than against those who try to enslave men by force of arms. Enemies, indeed, when noble and good men enslave some people, have often compelled many to become better through their discipline, and have made the rest of their lives easier for them; but such mistresses as these, torturing men's bodies, souls, and households, never cease doing so, so long as they hold rule over them.

div.head: Critobulus's supposed wealth, and true poverty
div.p: Critobulus then spoke to this effect: About such things I feel I have heard enough from what you say; but examining myself, I think I find myself reasonably in control of such things, so that if you were to advise me what I should do to increase my household, I do not think I would be hindered by these mistresses you speak of; so advise me boldly whatever good counsel you have -- unless indeed, Socrates, you have concluded that we are already rich enough, and think we have no further need of wealth?

For my part, said Socrates, if indeed you are speaking of me too, I do not think I have any need of wealth at all, but am rich enough; you, however, Critobulus, seem to me quite poor, and, by Zeus, there are times when I really pity you.

Critobulus laughed and said: And how much, by the gods, do you suppose your property would fetch if sold, Socrates, and how much mine? I think, said Socrates, that if I found a good buyer, I could very easily get five minas for my house together with all I possess; but yours I know for certain would fetch more than a hundred times that.

And knowing this, do you still think you have no need of wealth, while you pity me for my poverty? For my possessions, he said, are sufficient to provide me what I need; but as for the style you have wrapped yourself in and your reputation, even if what you now possess were increased threefold, I do not think it would be enough for you.

How so, indeed? said Critobulus. Socrates explained: First of all, I see that you are under obligation to offer many great sacrifices, or else, I think, neither gods nor men would put up with you; next, it falls to you to receive many guests, and to receive them magnificently; then again, to entertain your fellow citizens at dinner and do them good, or else be left without allies.

Moreover, I perceive that the city already lays heavy burdens on you -- the keeping of horses, the financing of choruses, gymnasiarchies, and public patronages -- and if war should come, I know they will lay on you the fitting-out of triremes and war-taxes so great that you will not easily bear them. And wherever you seem to fall short in any of these, I know the Athenians will punish you no less than if they caught you stealing what belongs to them.

Besides all this, I see you supposing yourself to be rich, and yet careless about contriving money, while giving your mind to boyish pursuits, as though it were open to you to indulge them. For these reasons I pity you, lest you suffer some irreparable evil and fall into great difficulty.

And for my part, if I should ever need anything more, you know as well as I that there are those who would supply it, so that, contributing quite little, they would flood my way of living with abundance; but your friends, though possessing far more than enough for their own establishments compared to you for yours, nonetheless look to you for benefit.

And Critobulus said: I cannot contradict any of this, Socrates; but it is high time you took charge of me, so that I do not truly become an object of pity. Hearing this, Socrates said: And does it not seem strange to you, Critobulus, that you do this to yourself -- that a little while ago, when I said I was rich, you laughed at me as one who did not even know what wealth was, and did not stop until you had proved me wrong and made me admit I possess not even a hundredth part of what you have; yet now you bid me take charge of you and see to it that you do not become truly poor?

I see, he said, Socrates, that you understand one wealth-producing skill -- how to create a surplus. I expect, then, that one who can create surplus from little could very easily create great surplus from much.

Do you not remember, then, just now in our conversation, when you would not let me even so much as murmur, saying that to a man who did not know how to use horses, horses were not wealth, nor land, nor sheep, nor silver, nor anything else that one did not know how to use? Now, revenues do come from such things -- but how do you suppose I could ever be trained to use any of these, seeing that from the very beginning I have never had anything of the sort?

But it seemed to us that even if a man happens to have no wealth, there is nonetheless such a thing as a science of household management. What, then, prevents you too from understanding it? Why, by Zeus, the very thing that would prevent a man from learning to play the pipes, if he had never himself owned pipes nor had another lend him his own to practise on; and that is exactly how it stands with me regarding household management.

For I have never owned the tools of the trade so as to learn on them, nor has anyone else ever let me manage their affairs, except you, who are now willing to do so. And surely those who are first learning to play the lyre ruin lyres in the process; so if I were to try learning household management on your estate, I might well ruin your household in the process.

To this Critobulus said: You are eager indeed, Socrates, to escape helping me in any way to bear more easily the burdens that are forced upon me. No, by Zeus, said Socrates, not I; rather, whatever I have I will explain to you quite readily.

And I think that if you had come to me for fire and I had none, and I had led you elsewhere to get it, you would not have blamed me; and if you had asked me for water and, not having any myself, I had led you elsewhere for that too, I know you would not have blamed me for that either; and if, wishing to learn music, I had shown you men far more skilled than myself in music who would even be grateful to you, should you be willing to learn from them, what fault could you still find with me for doing this?

None, justly, Socrates. Well then, I will show you, Critobulus, men far more skilled than I am in the very things you are now so eager to learn from me. I confess I have taken care to learn who among the people of this city are most knowledgeable in each field.

For once, having noticed that among men doing the very same work, some were extremely poor and others extremely rich, I was astonished, and it seemed to me worth investigating what the cause of this could be. And investigating, I found that this happens quite naturally.

For I saw that those who acted carelessly were penalised, while those who applied concentrated thought to their work I observed doing it faster, more easily, and more profitably. From such men, I think, you too, if you are willing, could learn and, if the god does not oppose you, become a formidably good man of business.

div.head: Order in the household, and the training of a wife
div.p: Hearing this, Critobulus said: Now indeed, Socrates, I will not let you go until you have demonstrated before these friends of ours what you promised. What then, Critobulus, said Socrates, if I show you first that some men build houses that are useless despite great expense, while others build houses that have everything necessary at far less expense -- would I seem to you to be demonstrating one of the works of household management?

Very much so indeed, said Critobulus. And what if, following on from this, I show you men who possess very many and various pieces of furniture, yet, when they need them, cannot use them and do not even know whether they are still intact, and are thereby much distressed themselves and cause much distress to their servants; while others, possessing no more but even less than these, have theirs ready at once whenever they need to use anything?

Is there, Socrates, any other cause of this than that in the first case each thing has been put down wherever it happened to fall, while in the second case each thing is set in its proper place? Yes, by Zeus, said Socrates; and not merely in any place that happens to be convenient, but in the place appropriate to it. You seem to me to be speaking of this too, said Critobulus, as belonging to household management.

Well then, what if I show you slaves too, in one house nearly all in chains, and yet frequently running away, and in another house unbound and willing both to work and to remain -- would this too not seem to you a worthy exhibit of the work of household management? Yes, by Zeus, said Critobulus, and very much so.

And what if I show you men farming similar farms, some declaring they are ruined by farming and are in difficulty, while others have everything they need from farming in abundance and excellence? Yes, by Zeus, said Critobulus. Perhaps, though, they spend not only on what is necessary, but also on what brings harm to themselves and their household.

There are perhaps some such men, said Socrates, but I am not speaking of these, but of those who claim to be farming, yet cannot even afford necessary expenses. And what would be the cause of that, Socrates? I will lead you to these men too, said Socrates, and you, by observing, will surely learn. Yes, by Zeus, he said, if I am able.

You must, then, watching them, make trial of your own understanding, to see whether you will recognise it. But as it is, I know you go to see comedies quite early in the morning and walk a very long way for it, and try eagerly to persuade me to go along and watch with you; but you have never once invited me to such a sight as this. Then I must seem ridiculous to you, Socrates.

Yes, by Zeus, far more ridiculous to yourself, he said. And what if I show you men ruined through horse-breeding, and others made quite wealthy through it and taking pride in the profit besides? I see both these kinds too, and know them, and am no more one of the profiting kind for all that.

For you watch them the way you watch tragic and comic actors -- not so that you may become a poet, I suppose, but so that you may enjoy something you see or hear; and perhaps that is right enough (since you do not wish to become a poet); but forced as you are to use horses, do you not think you are foolish if you do not take care not to remain an amateur at this pursuit, especially since the same horses are good both for use and for profitable resale?

Are you telling me to break in colts, Socrates? No, by Zeus, no more than to raise farmers by buying them as children; but there seem to me to be certain ages, both of horses and of men, at which they are immediately useful and improve further. And I can show you men who so treat their wedded wives that they have them as partners in increasing their households, while others treat them in a way that does the greatest possible harm.

And whom, Socrates, ought one to blame for this -- the man or the woman? If a sheep is generally in poor condition, said Socrates, we blame the shepherd; and if a horse generally misbehaves, we find fault with the horseman; as for the woman, if, being taught good things by her husband, she does wrong, perhaps the woman would justly bear the blame; but if the husband does not teach her good and noble conduct, but uses her while she is ignorant of it, would not the husband justly bear the blame?

But in any case, Critobulus, he said (for we are friends here present), you must be truthful with us. Is there anyone else to whom you entrust more serious matters than to your wife? To no one, he said. Is there anyone with whom you speak less than with your wife?

If not, then not with many, he said. And did you marry her when she was quite a young girl, who had seen and heard as little as possible? Very much so. Then it would be far more surprising if she knew anything of what she ought to say or do than if she made mistakes.

But as for those men you say have good wives, Socrates -- did they themselves train them? There is nothing like examining for oneself. And I will introduce you to Aspasia too, who will demonstrate all this to you with more expertise than I can.

But I hold that a wife who is a good partner in the household is fully counterbalancing to her husband in producing good; for property comes into the house for the most part through the husband's efforts, but it is spent for the most part through the wife's management; and when this is done well, households grow, but when it is done badly, households diminish.
I think I could show you, in the other arts too, if you think you need to see it, men who work worthily at each, achieving admirable results.

div.head: The gentleman farmer, and the King of Persia's example
div.p: But why must you show me all of them, Socrates? said Critobulus. For it is not easy to obtain skilled practitioners of every art, nor is it possible to become experienced in all of them; rather, show me those arts that seem finest and would suit me best to pursue, and their practitioners, and yourself help me all you can by teaching what pertains to them.

Well spoken, Critobulus, said Socrates. For indeed the arts called banausic (menial, workshop crafts) are both spoken against and, quite reasonably, held in very low esteem by our cities. For they ruin the bodies of those who work at them and those who oversee them, forcing them to sit and remain indoors, and some even to spend the whole day by the fire. And as their bodies become effeminate, their souls too grow much weaker.

And these so-called banausic occupations leave men least leisure to attend to their friends and their city as well. So such men appear to be poor both as friends and as defenders of their country. And indeed in some cities, especially those reputed good at war, it is not even permitted for any citizen to practise a banausic trade.

What occupations, then, Socrates, do you advise us to pursue? Shall we not be ashamed, said Socrates, to imitate the King of the Persians? For they say that he, counting farming and the art of war among the finest and most necessary pursuits, takes great care of both of these. Hearing this, Critobulus said:

And do you really believe this, Socrates -- that the King of the Persians takes any care at all for farming? We might discover, Critobulus, said Socrates, whether he takes any care of it by examining as follows. We agree, at any rate, that he takes strong care of matters of war, since he has ordered each governor, of whatever nations he receives tribute from, how many cavalry, archers, slingers, and shield-bearers he must maintain and provide with pay -- men capable both of controlling his subjects and, should enemies attack,

of defending the country; and besides these he maintains garrisons in the citadels. And the governor to whom this task is assigned provides pay for the garrison troops, while the King himself makes a yearly review of the mercenaries and the others ordered to be under arms, gathering them all together, except those stationed in the citadels, at the place called the muster; and those living around his own residence he inspects himself, while he sends trusted men to inspect those settled further away.

And whichever of the garrison-commanders, the captains of a thousand, or the satraps appear to have their appointed number complete and present them equipped with fine horses and arms, these commanders he honours with promotions and enriches with great gifts; but whichever of the commanders he finds neglecting their garrisons or profiteering, these he punishes severely, removing them from office and appointing other overseers in their place. In doing this concerning matters of war, then, he seems to us to take care of them beyond dispute.

Furthermore, whatever land he passes through, he inspects and assesses himself, and whatever he does not inspect himself, he sends trusted men to examine. And whichever of the governors he perceives to be presenting a well-populated country, with the land under active cultivation and full of the trees and crops each region produces, to these he adds further territory, adorns them with gifts, and honours them with seats of distinction; but whichever he sees with land lying idle and sparsely inhabited, whether through harshness, arrogance, or negligence, these he punishes, removing them from office and appointing other governors in their place.

Doing this, does he seem to care less that the land be kept in active cultivation by its inhabitants than that it be well guarded by its garrisons? And are the officials appointed for each of these two purposes not the same men, but different -- some ruling over the inhabitants and the labourers, and collecting tribute from them, others commanding the armed men and the garrisons?

And if the garrison-commander does not adequately defend the territory, the governor in charge of the inhabitants and their work accuses the garrison-commander, on the grounds that the people cannot work on account of the lack of protection; while if the garrison-commander keeps the fields at peace, but the governor presents the territory sparsely populated and idle, then in turn the garrison-commander accuses him.
For indeed, those who work the land badly can, as a rule, neither support the garrisons nor pay their tribute. And wherever a satrap is appointed, he takes charge of both these matters together.
At this Critobulus said: If, then, the King does these things, Socrates, he seems to me to care no less for the works of farming than for those of war.

Furthermore, said Socrates, in whatever countries he resides and to whatever he pays visits, he sees to it that there are gardens, the so-called paradises, full of everything fine and good that the earth is willing to grow, and in these he himself spends most of his time, whenever the season of the year does not prevent it.

By Zeus, said Critobulus, then it is necessary, Socrates, that wherever he himself spends his time, the paradises be arranged as beautifully as possible, cared for with trees and everything else fine that the earth produces.

Some say too, Socrates, said Critobulus -- and some say too, said Socrates, Critobulus, that whenever the King gives out gifts, he first calls in those who have proven themselves good in war, on the grounds that there is no use in much ploughing if there are none to defend it; and second, those who have best cultivated their territories and made them productive, saying that not even the brave could survive if there were none to work the land.

It is said that Cyrus too, who has become the most highly regarded of kings, once said to those summoned to receive gifts that he could rightly take the gifts due to both categories himself; for he claimed to be the best at cultivating land, and also at defending what had been cultivated.
Cyrus, then, said Critobulus, Socrates, took no less pride, if indeed he said this, in making lands productive and cultivating them than in being warlike.

Yes, by Zeus, said Socrates, and Cyrus, had he lived, seems likely to have become an excellent ruler; and he has given many other proofs of this, and in particular when he marched to fight his brother for the kingship, it is said that no one deserted from Cyrus to the King, but many tens of thousands deserted from the King to Cyrus.

And I count this too as a great proof of a ruler's excellence: that men should be willing to obey him and be willing to stand by him even in dangers. His friends both fought alongside him while he lived and died fighting around his body when he died, all except Ariaeus; and Ariaeus happened to be stationed on the left wing.

It is said, then, that this Cyrus, when Lysander came to bring him the gifts sent from the allies, treated him with friendliness in various ways -- as Lysander himself once related to a certain guest-friend at Megara -- and in particular showed him the garden at Sardis.

And when Lysander marvelled at how beautiful the trees were, planted at equal intervals, the rows of trees standing straight, all the angles well laid out, and many sweet scents accompanying them as they walked -- marvelling at this, he said: For my part, Cyrus, I marvel at all this for its beauty, but I admire far more the one who measured out and arranged each of these things for you --
and hearing this, Cyrus, it is said, was delighted and said: Well, Lysander, I myself both measured out and arranged all of this, and some of it, he said, I even planted myself.

And Lysander, they say, looking at him, and seeing the beauty of the garments he wore, and perceiving their fragrance, and the beauty of his necklaces and bracelets and all the other adornment he had, said: What do you mean, Cyrus? Did you truly plant some of this with your own hands?

And Cyrus answered: Does this surprise you, Lysander? I swear to you by Mithras, whenever I am in good health, I never dine before I have worked up a sweat, either practising some art of war or of farming, or always striving eagerly at some one pursuit or other.
And Lysander himself said that, hearing this, he took his hand and said: You seem to me, Cyrus, to be rightly blessed with good fortune; for you are happy because you are a good man.

div.head: In praise of farming
div.p: I tell you this, Critobulus, said Socrates, because not even the most fortunate of men can keep away from farming. For the practice of it seems to be at once a kind of pleasure, an increase of the household, and a training of the body in whatever befits a free man.
For, in the first place, the earth bears for those who work it the things by which men live, and it further provides the things by which they take pleasure;

then it provides, along with the sweetest fragrances and sights, whatever men use to adorn altars, statues, and themselves; then it produces many delicacies, some of which grow naturally, others which it nourishes -- for the art of herding sheep too is joined to farming, so that men can both please the gods with sacrifices and make use of the flocks themselves.

And though providing good things in the greatest abundance, it does not allow them to be taken with softness, but accustoms men to endure the cold of winter and the heat of summer. And it strengthens those who work with their own hands by exercising them through their labour, while it makes manly those who farm with active oversight, waking them early and forcing them to move vigorously; for both in the countryside and in the city, the most urgent tasks are always tied to their proper season.

Then again, whether a man wishes to help defend the city on horseback, farming is the most capable of maintaining his horse; or on foot, it makes the body vigorous; and the land also stirs men on somewhat to love hunting, providing easy feeding for dogs and nourishing wild game alongside its crops.

And the horses and dogs, benefited in turn by farming, benefit the land in return: the horse carrying its master early to the work of overseeing it, and allowing him to leave late, and the dogs keeping wild beasts from damaging the crops and the flocks, and helping to keep the lonely places safe.
The land, too, by nourishing crops in the open field for whoever conquers there to take, spurs men on to defend their country with arms.

And what art provides men more fit for running, throwing, and jumping than farming? What art rewards its workers more generously in return? What art welcomes its diligent tender more gladly, offering, as he approaches, whatever he needs to take?

What art receives guests more generously? Where is it easier to spend the winter with abundant fire and warm baths than in the countryside? Where is it pleasanter to spend the summer amid waters, breezes, and shade than in the fields?

What other art offers more fitting first-fruits to the gods, or provides for fuller festivals? What art is dearer to servants, sweeter to a wife, more longed-for by children, or more welcome to friends?
It seems astonishing to me if any free man has acquired a possession sweeter than this, or found any pursuit pleasanter or more beneficial to life.
Furthermore, the earth, being a goddess, also teaches justice to those able to learn from her; for to those who serve her best, she gives back the most good things in return.

And if those engaged in farming, trained vigorously and manfully, should ever be deprived of their work by the multitude of invading armies, being well prepared in both soul and body, unless a god prevents it, they can go and take from the lands of those preventing them what they need to be fed; and often in war it is even safer to seek one's food with weapons than with farming tools.
Farming also trains men to help one another; for one must go against the enemy together with other men, and the working of the land too is done together with other men.

The man who intends to farm well, then, must make his workers eager and willing to obey; and the man leading an army against the enemy must contrive the very same things, rewarding those who do what good men ought to do, and punishing those who are disorderly.
And the farmer must often exhort his workers no less than the general his soldiers; and slaves need good hopes no less than free men -- indeed even more, so that they may be willing to remain.

And that man spoke well who said that farming is the mother and nurse of the other arts. For when farming flourishes, all the other arts thrive too, but wherever the land is forced to lie fallow, the other arts are nearly extinguished as well, both on land and sea.

Hearing this, Critobulus said: This, Socrates, seems to me well said; but that most of what belongs to farming is beyond human foresight is plain: for hail, and frost, and droughts, and excessive rains, and blights, and many other things often destroy what has been well planned and well executed; and sometimes disease coming upon sheep that have been very well raised destroys them most wretchedly.

Hearing this, Socrates said: But I thought, Critobulus, that you knew the gods are no less masters of the works of farming than of those of war. And you see, I think, those engaged in war, before their military actions, propitiating the gods and asking through sacrifices and omens what they should do and what they should not;

and concerning the works of farming, do you think one should be any less eager to appease the gods? Know well, he said, that men of sound mind serve the gods on behalf of both wet and dry crops alike, and on behalf of cattle, horses, and sheep, and indeed on behalf of all their possessions.

div.head: The search for the true gentleman: Ischomachus
div.p: But this, Socrates, said he, you seem to me to say well, bidding us try to begin every work with the gods, since the gods are no less masters of the works of peace than of war. We shall try, then, to do so. But now go on and continue explaining household management from where you left off, since now, having heard what you have said, I feel I already see somewhat more clearly than before what I ought to do to make a living.
What then, said Socrates, if we first went back over what we have already agreed upon, so that, if we can, we might try to go through the rest in the same spirit of agreement?

It is pleasant, at any rate, said Critobulus, just as when men share property they go through the accounting without dispute, so too, sharing in the conversation, to go through what we discuss in agreement with one another.

Well then, said Socrates, household management seemed to us to be the name of a certain branch of knowledge, and this knowledge appeared to be that by which men are able to increase their households, and a household appeared to us to be the same as one's entire property, and we said that property was whatever was beneficial to each man for his life, and things beneficial turned out to be all those things a man knew how to use.

Now it seemed to us that it was not possible to learn all branches of knowledge, and we joined the cities in disapproving of the so-called banausic arts, because they seem both to ruin the body and to break down the soul.

And we said the clearest proof of this would be this: if, when enemies invade the country, one were to seat the farmers and the craftsmen separately and ask each group whether they think it better to defend the land or to abandon the land and guard the walls instead.

For in this way we thought that those concerned with the land would vote to defend it, while the craftsmen would vote not to fight, but, as they have been trained, to sit still, neither labouring nor risking themselves.
And we concluded that for a noble and good man, farming is the best occupation and branch of knowledge, from which men provide themselves with necessities.

For this occupation seemed to be the easiest to learn and the pleasantest to work at, and to make the body most beautiful and vigorous, while leaving the soul the least amount of time taken up, so that a man may still attend to his friends and his city.

And farming seemed to us to spur men on somewhat to courage as well, by producing and nourishing the necessities of life outside the fortifications for those who work at it. For these reasons, too, this way of life is held in the highest esteem by our cities, since it seems to produce the best citizens and those most well-disposed to the community.

And Critobulus said: That it is finest and best and pleasantest to make one's living from farming, Socrates, I feel I am quite sufficiently persuaded; but as to what you said, that you had learned the causes both of why some farm in such a way as to have abundance of what they need from farming, and of why some work in such a way that farming does not profit them, I would gladly hear both of these from you, so that we may do what is good and avoid what is harmful.

What then, Critobulus, said Socrates, if I told you from the beginning how I once came to associate with a man who seemed to me to be truly one of those men on whom the name is rightly bestowed of being a gentleman (kalos kagathos)? I would very much like to hear that, said Critobulus, since I too aspire to become worthy of that name.

I will tell you, then, said Socrates, how I came to inquire into this. It took me very little time to go around and observe the works held to be fine among good carpenters, good metalworkers, good painters, sculptors, and the like.
But my soul greatly desired to meet with one of those who hold this solemn name, gentleman, to examine just what they did to be deemed worthy of being so called.

And first, because the word beautiful (kalos) is attached to good (agathos), whenever I saw someone handsome I would approach him and try to observe whether I might see the good attached anywhere to the beautiful.

But it did not turn out to be so; rather I found that some, it seemed to me, had beautiful forms but were quite base in soul. It seemed best to me, then, to set aside handsome appearance and go instead to one of those actually called gentlemen.
So then, since I heard Ischomachus spoken of by everyone -- men and women, foreigners and citizens -- as being called a gentleman, it seemed good to me to try to make his acquaintance.

div.head: Ischomachus trains his wife: the queen bee
div.p: Seeing him once, then, sitting in the Stoa of Zeus Eleutherios, since he seemed to me to be at leisure, I went up to him, and, sitting down beside him, I said: Why, Ischomachus, are you sitting here at leisure, you who are not much accustomed to leisure? For I generally see you either doing something, or at least not entirely idle in the marketplace.

You would not see me now either, Socrates, said Ischomachus, if I had not agreed to wait here for some guests. And when you are not doing something of that sort, by the gods, I said, where do you spend your time and what do you do? For I am very eager to learn from you what you do to be called a gentleman, since you do not spend your time indoors, nor does the condition of your body appear to be that of one who does.

And Ischomachus, laughing at the question of what he did to be called a gentleman, and seeming pleased, as it appeared to me, said: Well, I do not know whether, when people discuss me with you, they call me by that name; certainly, at any rate, when I am called upon for an exchange of property to fund a trireme or a chorus, no one, he said, looks for the gentleman, but they simply call for me by name, Ischomachus, son of so-and-so. Now then, Socrates, he said, to what you asked me, I do not spend any time at all indoors. For indeed, he said, my wife is quite capable of managing what is in the house by herself.

But this too, Ischomachus, I said, I would very gladly ask you about: did you yourself train your wife to be as she should be, or did you receive her from her father and mother already knowing how to manage her proper duties?

And how, Socrates, he said, could I have received her already knowing anything, seeing that she came to me when she was not yet fifteen years old, and had lived the previous time under the greatest care that she might see as little as possible, hear as little as possible, and ask as little as possible?

Do you not think it is enough if she came knowing only how to take wool and produce a garment from it, and having seen how spinning work is given out to the maidservants? For as far as matters of appetite are concerned, Socrates, she came very well trained indeed -- which seems to me the greatest instruction of all, both for a man and for a woman.
But the rest, I said, Ischomachus, did you yourself train your wife so as to be capable of the things she ought to attend to? No, by Zeus, said Ischomachus,

not before I had offered sacrifice and prayed that I might succeed in teaching, and she in learning, what was best for us both. And so, I said, did your wife join you in the sacrifice and share in the same prayer? Very much so, said Ischomachus, promising many things to the gods that she would become what she ought to be, and it was quite clear that she would not be careless of what she was taught.

By the gods, Ischomachus, I said, tell me, what did you begin by teaching her first? For I would listen to you telling this more gladly than if you told me of the finest athletic or equestrian contest.

And Ischomachus answered: Well, Socrates, when she was already tame with me and tractable enough to converse with, I asked her something like this: Tell me, wife, have you by now considered why it was that I took you, and your parents gave you, to me?

For that there was no shortage of someone else with whom we might have slept, you know as well as I. But I, deliberating on my own behalf, and your parents on yours, as to whom we might get as the best partner for household and children, I chose you, and your parents, as it seems, chose me, from among the possible candidates.

Now if god should ever grant us children, we shall deliberate then about how we shall raise them as well as possible; for this too is a good thing shared between us, to gain the best possible allies and support for our old age.

But as things stand now, this household here is shared between us. For I declare into the common stock everything I have, and you likewise have put into the common stock everything you brought with you. And we need not calculate which of us has contributed more in number, but rather know well that whichever of us proves the better partner, that one contributes what is of greater worth.
And my wife answered me on this, Socrates: But how could I help you? What is my ability? Why, everything depends on you; my mother told me my task was to be sensible and self-controlled.

Yes, by Zeus, I said, wife, and my father told me the same. But it belongs to sensible people, both husband and wife, to act in such a way that their property will be in the best possible state, and that as much more as possible will be added to it by fair and just means.
And what do you see, said my wife, that I could do to help increase the household? Why, by Zeus, I said, try, as best you can, to do what the gods have made you capable of and what the law approves.
And what is that? she said. I think, I said, things not of the least importance -- unless indeed the queen bee in the hive too presides over tasks of the least worth.
For to me, wife, the gods too seem to have coupled together, with great deliberation, that pair called female and male, so that it might be most beneficial to each of them for their partnership.

For, first of all, this pair exists together so that the various races of living creatures may not die out, by begetting offspring with one another; then, from this pair, at least for human beings, is provided the means of having support in old age; and further, the way of life for human beings is not, as it is for cattle, lived in the open air, but plainly requires shelter.

It is necessary, however, for those men who are going to have anything to bring into the shelter, that there be someone to do the work out in the open; for ploughing, sowing, planting, and pasturing are all works done in the open, and from these come the necessities of life.

And again, once these have been brought into the shelter, there is need of someone to keep them safe and to do the work that requires shelter. Shelter is needed too for the rearing of newborn children, and shelter is needed for the making of bread from the grain; and likewise the working of wool into clothing needs shelter too.

Since, then, both of these -- the outdoor and the indoor tasks -- require work and attention, the god, it seems to me, from the very beginning made ready the nature of the woman for the indoor works and cares, and that of the man for the outdoor ones.

For he equipped the man's body and soul to be more capable of enduring cold and heat, journeys and military campaigns; and so he assigned to him the outdoor works; but to the woman, since he made her body less capable of enduring these things, it seems to me the god has assigned the indoor works.
And knowing that he had implanted in the woman, and assigned to her, the nourishing of newborn children, he also allotted her a greater share of affection for newborn infants than to the man.

And since he also assigned to the woman the guarding of what is brought in, the god, knowing that for guarding it is no bad thing to have a fearful soul, allotted a greater share of fear to the woman than to the man. And knowing that the one with the outdoor works would also need to defend against wrongdoers, he allotted to him, in turn, a greater share of boldness.

But because both need to give and to take, he placed memory and diligence equally at the disposal of both, so that you could not distinguish which of the two sexes, the female or the male, has the advantage in these.

And he placed self-control over what is needful equally at the disposal of both, and the god gave power to whichever of the two, whether husband or wife, should prove better, to carry off the greater share of this good.

And because their natures are not equally well suited to all the same things, for this very reason they have greater need of one another, and the pairing has become more beneficial to itself, since what the one lacks, the other is able to supply.
Knowing these things, then, wife, that these tasks have been assigned to each of us by god, we must try, each of us, to carry out as best we can what falls to each.

And the law too approves these arrangements, said my wife, coupling husband and wife together; and just as god made them partners in their children, so the law establishes them as partners in the household. And the law declares to be honourable those things which the god made each of the two naturally more capable of. For it is more honourable for the woman to remain indoors than to be out of doors, but for the man it is more shameful to remain indoors than to attend to what is outside.

And if anyone acts contrary to what the god has made him naturally fit for, perhaps, being somewhat disorderly, he does not escape the notice of the gods, and pays the penalty either for neglecting his own proper work, or for doing the work belonging to the woman.

It seems to me, I said, that the queen bee too labours at such tasks as these, assigned to her by the god. And what kind of tasks, said she, does the queen bee have that resemble the tasks I must perform?

Because, I said, she, remaining in the hive, does not allow the bees to be idle, but sends out to work those that must work outside, and she knows and receives whatever each of them brings in, and keeps it safe until there is need to use it. And when the time comes to use it, she distributes to each her fair share.

And she also presides over the honeycombs woven inside, that they be woven well and quickly, and she takes care of the brood that is born, that it be reared; and when it has been reared and the young bees are fit for work, she sends them out to found a colony under the leadership of one of their number.

Then shall I too, said my wife, have to do these things? You will indeed have to, I said, remain indoors, and send out those of the servants whose work is outside, and superintend those whose work must be done indoors,

and you must receive what is brought in, and distribute what portion of it needs to be spent, and foresee and guard against the yearly store being spent within a month. And when wool is brought in to you, you must see to it that garments are made for those who need them. And you must also take care that the dry grain is made fit and good to eat.

One of the duties belonging to you, however, said I, will perhaps seem rather thankless: whichever of the servants falls sick, you must see to it that all of them are cared for. Yes, by Zeus, said my wife, and most gratifying indeed it will be, if those well cared for are going to be grateful and better disposed than before.

And I, said Ischomachus, admiring her answer, said: Is it not, wife, through such forethought as this that the bees too are so disposed toward their queen in the hive, that whenever she leaves, not one of the bees thinks it right to be left behind, but they all follow her?

And my wife answered me: I should be surprised, she said, if the leader's tasks did not apply more to you than to me; for my guarding and distributing of what is indoors would seem ridiculous, I think, if you did not take care that something be brought in from outside.

And ridiculous in turn, I said, would be my bringing-in, if there were no one to keep safe what is brought in. Do you not see, I said, how those said to be drawing water into a leaking jar are pitied, because they seem to be labouring in vain? Yes, by Zeus, said my wife, for indeed they are wretched, if that is what they are doing.

But other duties too, wife, I said, will become pleasant to you in their own right, whenever you take a woman unskilled in wool-work and make her skilled, so that she becomes worth twice as much to you; and whenever you take a woman unskilled in housekeeping and service and make her skilled, trustworthy, and capable, so that she becomes worth anything at all; and whenever it is in your power to reward those who are sensible and beneficial to your household, but to punish anyone who proves wicked;

and, sweetest of all, if you should show yourself better than I am, and make me your servant, and you need not fear that as your years advance you will become less honoured in the household, but may be confident that as you grow older, the more you become a better partner to me and a better guardian of the household for our children, so much the more honoured you will be in the household.

For it is not through youthful bloom, I said, but through virtue in the conduct of life, that what is fine and good increases for human beings. Such, Socrates, I believe, is what I recall having discussed with her at first.

div.head: The order of household goods, and the ship's mate
div.p: And did you perceive, Ischomachus, I said, that she was in any way stirred to greater diligence by this? Yes, by Zeus, said Ischomachus, and I know too that she was stung and blushed deeply, because, when I asked for something that had been brought in, she was unable to give it to me.

And I, seeing her distressed, said: Do not be at all discouraged, wife, that you cannot give me what I happen to be asking for. This is indeed a kind of poverty, plainly, to lack what one needs to use; but this kind of want -- to seek something and not be able to find it -- is less distressing than never even to seek it at all, knowing from the start that it does not exist. But indeed, I said, none of this is your fault, but mine, for handing things over to you without arranging where each thing ought to be kept, so that you might know where to put things and where to take them from.

There is nothing, wife, so useful or so fine for human beings as order. For a chorus too is made up of human beings; but when each performer does whatever he happens to feel like, it appears a kind of confusion, unpleasant to watch, whereas when they act and sing in an ordered way, these very same people seem worth both watching and hearing.

And an army too, wife, I said, when disorderly, is the most confused thing to see, most easily overcome by the enemy, and most inglorious and useless a sight for its friends -- a donkey mixed in among hoplites, baggage-carriers, light troops, cavalry, and wagons -- for how could they even march, if, being arranged this way, they hinder one another, the walker blocking the runner, the runner the man standing still, the wagon the horseman, the donkey the wagon, the baggage-carrier the hoplite?

And if they should need to fight, how could they fight, arranged in this way? For those of them who must flee before the enemy's advance are quite capable, in their flight, of trampling down those bearing weapons.

But an army in order is the finest sight for friends to see, and most difficult for enemies to face. For what friend would not gladly behold hoplites marching in ranks in good order? Who would not admire cavalry riding by squadrons? What enemy would not be afraid, seeing well-arranged hoplites, cavalry, peltasts, archers, and slingers, following their commanders in good order?

And even on the march, though there be many tens of thousands, if they are in order, they all proceed just like a single man, quietly one after another; for those behind always advance into the space that opens before them.

And why else is a trireme crowded with men fearsome to enemies and a fine sight for friends, other than because it sails swiftly? And why else are the men on board no trouble to one another, other than because, in order, they sit down, in order lean forward, in order lean back, and in order embark and disembark?

Disorder seems to me to be much like what would happen if a farmer were to throw barley, wheat, and beans together into one heap, and then, whenever he needed either barley-cake, bread, or a vegetable dish, he had to pick them apart, instead of simply taking them already sorted and using them.

So you too, wife, if you wish to avoid this confusion, and to know exactly what you have, and to be able to take readily whatever you need, and to give it to me graciously whenever I ask -- let us choose a proper place for each thing to have, and, having established each in that place, let us teach the housekeeper to take things from there and to put them back there again; and in this way we shall know both what is safe and what is not; for the place itself will miss what is not there, and the eye will notice what needs attention, and knowing exactly where each thing is will quickly put it into our hands, so that we never have trouble using it.

I once thought I saw the finest and most exact arrangement of equipment, Socrates, when I went aboard the great Phoenician merchant ship to see it. For I observed the greatest quantity of gear, all separated out, in the smallest of vessels.

For a ship is anchored and put out to sea by means of a great many wooden and woven implements; it sails by means of a great many things called the rigging; it is armed against enemy vessels with many devices; it carries around many weapons for the crew; and it brings whatever equipment the men use for their mess in each division; and besides all this it is full of the cargo that the ship's captain carries for profit.

And all the things I mention, he said, were lying in a space not much larger than a room fit for ten couches. And I observed that each of these, so placed, neither obstructed one another, nor needed searching for, nor was hard to get to, nor difficult to loosen, so as to cause delay when something was needed quickly.

And I found that the captain's assistant, the man called the look-out, knew the place of each thing so well that even away from the ship he could say where each thing lay and how many there were, no less than a man who knows his letters could say how many letters are in the name Socrates, and where each one is placed.

I even saw this same man, said Ischomachus, in his free time examining everything used on the ship. And, marvelling at his inspection, I asked him what he was doing. And he said: I am examining, stranger, in case something should happen, how things lie on the ship, or whether anything is out of place, or lies in an awkward position.

For there is no chance, he said, when god sends a storm at sea, either to search for what is needed, or to hand it over lying in an awkward position. For god threatens and punishes the careless. It is quite enough if he merely does not destroy those who are not at fault; but if he even saves those who serve him well, great thanks indeed are owed to the gods.

So I, having observed this precise arrangement, said to my wife that it would be quite stupid of us if men on ships, even small ones, find room for things, and, though tossed about violently, still keep good order, and though badly frightened, still find what is needed to take -- while we, with separate large storerooms for everything in the house, and the house standing firmly on the ground, should fail to find a good and easily discoverable place for each thing -- how would that not show great folly on our part?
How good it is, then, to have equipment properly arranged, and how easy it is to find a place for each thing in a house that suits it, has now been said;

and how fine it appears, when shoes are lined up in a row, of whatever kind they are, how fine it is to see garments kept separate, of whatever kind, how fine to see bedding, how fine bronze vessels, how fine what belongs to the table, and how fine too -- what everyone, not the solemn but the witty man, would laugh at most of all -- that even cooking pots appear graceful when placed in neat order --

and everything else, from this, already appears more beautiful when set out according to order; for each set of things appears like a chorus, and the space in the middle of all of them appears beautiful too, with each thing removed out of the way; just as a circular chorus is not only itself a beautiful sight, but its middle too appears beautiful and clear --

and if what I say is true, wife, I said, it is possible to make trial of these things without any loss or great effort. Nor need you be discouraged, wife, I said, thinking it hard to find someone who will learn the places and remember to put everything back accordingly.

For we know, I suppose, that the whole city has ten thousand times as much of everything as we do; and yet, whichever of the servants you order to go and buy something for you from the market and bring it back, none of them will be at a loss, but every one of them will know where he must go to fetch each thing. And the cause of this, I said, is nothing else than that each thing lies in an established place.

But when looking for a person, and that too sometimes a person who is himself looking for you in return, one would often give up before finding him. And the cause of this, again, is nothing else than that there is no fixed place where each person is to be found waiting. Such, then, is what I recall discussing with her about the arrangement and use of household goods.

div.head: Assigning storerooms, and appointing a housekeeper
div.p: And what then? Did the woman seem to you, Ischomachus, I said, to be at all won over by what you took such trouble to teach her? What else, he said, but that she promised to take care of it, and was clearly delighted, as though she had found some resource out of helplessness, and she asked me to arrange things as quickly as I had described, in just the way I had spoken of.

And how then, Ischomachus, I said, did you arrange things for her? What else, but that I thought it best first to show her the capabilities of the house itself. For it is not decorated with elaborate ornament, Socrates, but the rooms have been built with precisely this in mind: that they might be the most fitting receptacles possible for whatever was going to be kept in them; so that the rooms themselves called for what was appropriate to be in each.

For the inner chamber, being in a secure position, called for the most valuable bedding and furniture; the dry parts of the storerooms called for the grain; the cool parts, the wine; and the bright parts, whatever work and equipment needed light.

And I showed her too the living-quarters for the people, decorated to be cool in summer and warm in winter. And I showed her the whole house, that it opens toward the south, so that it is clear it is sunny in winter and shady in summer.

I showed her too the women's quarters, marked off from the men's quarters by a bolted door, so that nothing that ought not be carried out from within, and so that the servants should not have children without our knowledge; for those who are good, once they have children, generally become more well-disposed, but the wicked, once paired off, become more resourceful in wrongdoing.

When we had gone through all this, he said, we then sorted the furniture by kind. We began, he said, by gathering together whatever we use for sacrifices. After this we divided out the woman's ornaments used for festivals, the man's clothing for festivals and war, and bedding for the women's quarters, bedding for the men's quarters, women's shoes, men's shoes.

One category was for weapons, another for wool-working tools, another for bread-making tools, another for cooking tools, another for what pertains to the bath, another for kneading-troughs, another for what pertains to the table. And all these we divided out, both what is used continually and what is used for feasts.

We also set apart what is spent monthly, and separately what has been calculated for the whole year set aside; for in this way it is less likely to escape notice how it will come out in the end. And when we had sorted all the furniture by kind, we carried each item to its appropriate place.

After this, whatever equipment the servants use daily -- such as tools for bread-making, cooking, wool-working, and anything else of that sort -- these we showed to the very people who use them, indicating where they should be put, and handed them over, instructing them to keep them intact;

but whatever we use for festivals, for entertaining guests, or for occasional occurrences, these we handed over to the housekeeper, and, having shown her their places and counted and listed each item, we told her to give out to whoever needed each thing, and to remember what she gave to whom, and, when receiving it back, to put it back again in the very place from which she had taken each item.

We appointed the housekeeper after examining who among the household seemed to us most self-controlled with respect to food, wine, sleep, and relations with men; and besides this, she who seemed to have the best memory, and the foresight not to incur any harm from us through negligence, and to consider how, by pleasing us in some way, she might be rewarded by us in turn.

We also taught her to be well-disposed toward us, sharing our joys with her when we rejoiced, and calling on her to share in whatever was distressing. We also trained her to be eager to help increase the household, making her recognize its affairs and giving her a share in its success.

And we instilled a sense of justice in her too, by holding the just in greater honour than the unjust, and by showing that the just live in greater wealth and freedom than the unjust; and we placed her herself among that rank.

And on top of all this, Socrates, said Ischomachus, I told my wife that none of it would be of any use unless she herself took care that order be maintained in each thing. I taught her too that even in well-governed cities, it does not seem enough for the citizens to write good laws, but they also appoint guardians of the laws, who, overseeing them, praise whoever acts according to the laws, and, if anyone acts contrary to the laws, penalize him.

I bid my wife, then, to consider herself the guardian of the laws of the household, and to review the furniture, whenever it seemed good to her, just as the garrison-commander reviews his sentries, and to assess whether everything is in good condition, just as the Council assesses horses and horsemen, and to praise and honour whoever deserved it, insofar as it lay in her power, and to reprove and punish whoever needed it.

Besides this, I taught her that she should not be justly aggrieved if I assigned her more tasks concerning the household property than to the servants, by pointing out that the servants have a share in the master's property only to the extent of carrying, tending, or guarding it, and none of them may use anything unless the master gives it to him; but everything belongs to the master, to use as he pleases.
I showed her, then, that whoever gains the greatest benefit when things are kept safe, and suffers the greatest loss when they are ruined, has the greatest claim to taking care of them.

Well then, Ischomachus, I said, how did your wife respond, having heard all this? What else, he said, but that she told me I was mistaken if I thought I was giving her hard instructions in teaching her that she must take care of our property. It would be harder for her, she said, if I ordered her to neglect her own affairs than if she had to take care of our household goods.

For it seems, he said, to be natural -- just as it is more pleasant for a sensible woman to take care of her own children than to neglect them -- so too, for a sensible woman, it is more pleasant to take care of possessions that are her own and that give her joy, than to neglect them.

div.head: On dress and true beauty
div.p: And hearing, said Socrates, that his wife had answered him this way, I said: By Hera, Ischomachus, you are demonstrating quite a manly way of thinking in your wife. And I have other things too, said Ischomachus, quite high-minded of her, that I wish to relate to you, which she took to heart at once, after hearing them just once from me. What sort of things? I said; tell me, since I would much rather learn about the virtue of a living woman than if Zeuxis showed me a beautiful woman he had painted in a picture.

Then Ischomachus said: Well, Socrates, having seen her once heavily made up with white lead, so as to seem fairer than she was, and with much rouge, so as to appear rosier than the truth, and wearing high shoes, so as to seem taller than she naturally was --

Tell me, wife, I said, would you judge me a more worthy partner in our property if I showed you our actual possessions, and neither boasted that I had more than I really do, nor concealed any part of what I have -- or if I tried to deceive you by saying I had more than I really do, and by showing you counterfeit silver, gilded necklaces, and fading purple cloth, claiming they were genuine?

And she at once took me up and said: Hush! May you never become such a man! For I could never love you from my heart if you were like that. Well, I said, have we not come together as partners in our bodies too? So people say, at least, she said.

Which way, then, said I, would I seem to you a more worthy partner in body -- if I tried to present my own body to you, taking care that it be healthy and strong, and so, being truly in good condition, would actually appear well-complexioned to you -- or if I smeared myself with red ochre and painted my eyes with flesh-coloured cosmetic, and presented myself to you and lived with you deceiving you, giving you to see and touch ochre instead of my own skin?

As for me, she said, I would take no more pleasure in touching ochre than in touching you, nor would I take more pleasure in looking at the colour of cosmetic than at your own, nor at eyes painted with dye than at your own healthy eyes.

Believe of me too, then, wife, said Ischomachus, that I take no more pleasure in the colour of white lead or rouge than in your own; but just as the gods have made horses most pleasing to horses, cattle to cattle, and sheep to sheep, so human beings think a clean human body the most pleasant of all --

and these deceptions might perhaps be able to fool outsiders without being found out, but those who live together are inevitably caught, if ever they try to deceive one another; for they are caught either getting up from bed before they have prepared themselves, or they are betrayed by sweat, or found out by tears, or truly exposed by bathing.

What then, by the gods, I said, did she answer to this? What else, he said, but that from then on she never again practised anything of that sort, but tried to show herself clean and becomingly dressed. And she also asked me whether I had any advice to give her so that she might truly appear beautiful, rather than merely seem to.

And I indeed, Socrates, he said, advised her not to sit around always like a slave, but to try, with the gods' help, to take up a mistress's role -- standing at the loom, to teach what she knew better than another, and to learn what she knew worse; to oversee the bread-maker; to stand by the housekeeper as she measures things out; and to go about inspecting whether everything is in its proper place. For this seemed to me to be at once a form of exercise and a kind of walk.

And I said it was also good exercise to wet and knead dough, to shake out and fold garments and bedding. I said that, exercising in this way, she would eat with more pleasure, be healthier, and appear more truly well-complexioned.

And a wife's appearance, when compared with that of a servant, being cleaner and more becomingly dressed, is more stirring, especially when she willingly gives her favours instead of being compelled to serve.

But women who always sit around solemnly expose themselves to comparison with those who use cosmetics and deceit. And now, Socrates, he said, know well that my wife lives arranged in just the way I taught her and am now telling you.

div.head: Ischomachus's daily round: horse, farm, and public duties
div.p: At this, I said: Ischomachus, I feel I have heard enough for the moment about your wife's tasks, and they are quite worthy of praise for both of you. But now tell me your own tasks, so that you, having related the things for which you are well regarded, may take pleasure in it, and I, having thoroughly heard and learned the works of a gentleman, may, if I am able, be very grateful to you.
Why yes, by Zeus, Socrates, said Ischomachus, I will gladly relate to you what I continually make it my practice to do, so that you may correct me if you think I am doing anything wrong.

But how, I said, could I justly correct a man already made into a gentleman -- and that too being a man who is thought to be a chatterer and a measurer of air, and, what seems the most foolish accusation of all, is called poor?

And indeed, Ischomachus, I would have been quite despondent at this reproach, had I not recently, meeting the horse belonging to Nicias the foreigner, seen many spectators following it, and heard many people talking a great deal about it; and so I went up and asked the groom whether the horse had much money.

And he, looking at me as though I were not quite sane in my question, said: And how could money belong to a horse? At this I brightened up, hearing that it is indeed permitted even for a poor horse to become a good one, if it has a naturally good spirit.

So then, since it is permitted for me too to become a good man, tell me your own tasks fully, so that, listening, I may try, as far as I am able to learn, to imitate you starting from tomorrow. For indeed, I said, it is a good day to begin virtue.
You are joking, Socrates, said Ischomachus, but nonetheless I will tell you what I try, as best I can, to practise as I pass through life.

For since I believe I have come to understand that the gods have not made it lawful for men to fare well without knowing what they ought to do and taking care that it be accomplished, but that to those who are prudent and diligent they grant happiness, while to others they do not, so I begin by serving the gods, and I try to act in such a way that, praying, it may be lawful for me to obtain health, strength of body, honour in the city, goodwill among friends, honourable safety in war, and wealth increasing honourably.

And hearing this, I said: Do you really care, Ischomachus, about being wealthy, and, having much money, having much trouble taking care of it? Yes indeed, said Ischomachus, I do care about the things you ask; for it seems pleasant to me, Socrates, to honour the gods magnificently, to help friends if they are in need of anything, and to see to it that the city is not left unadorned, as far as it depends on me, for lack of money.

And these are indeed fine things you speak of, Ischomachus, I said, and belonging to a truly capable man. For why not? Since there are many people who cannot live without needing help from others, while many are content if they can provide enough for themselves; but those who are able not only to manage their own household but also to accumulate a surplus, so as to adorn their city and relieve their friends -- how should we not consider these men to be men of substance and strength?

But many of us, I said, are able to praise such men; tell me, however, Ischomachus, starting from where you began, how do you take care of your health? How is it lawful for you to have strength of body and to come safely home from war as well? As for the making of money, I said, we can hear about that afterward.

Well, said Ischomachus, all these things seem to me, Socrates, to follow from one another. For when a man has enough to eat, it seems to me that health is more likely to remain with him if he exerts himself rightly, and strength is more likely to be added to him if he exerts himself, and it is more likely he will come through war safely if he practises what is needed for it, and it is more likely his household will increase if he is properly diligent and does not grow soft.

But up to this point, I said, Ischomachus, I follow you, that by exerting oneself, taking care, and practising, a man is more likely to attain these good things; but what sort of exertion do you use for good bodily condition and strength, and how do you practise for war, and how do you take care of creating a surplus so as to help your friends and strengthen your city -- these things I would gladly learn.

Well then, Socrates, said Ischomachus, I am accustomed to rise from bed while I might still find someone I need to see still at home; and if there is anything I need to attend to in the city, I use this errand as my walk.

But if there is nothing pressing to do in the city, the boy leads my horse out to the country, and I make my walk along the road to the farm -- which is perhaps better, Socrates, than if I were walking about in a covered gallery.

And when I arrive at the farm, wherever I find them planting, fallowing, sowing, or bringing in the crop, I inspect how each task is being done, and I make changes if I have anything better to suggest than the current method.

After this, as a rule, I mount my horse and ride, as far as I am able, in a manner as similar as possible to the riding necessary in war, avoiding neither slopes nor descents nor ditches nor watercourses -- taking care all the same, as far as possible, while doing this, not to lame the horse.

When this is done, the boy rolls the horse and takes it home, bringing back with him from the farm whatever we may need in the city. I, meanwhile, walk part of the way, and part of the way I return home running, and then scrape myself down. Then I take my midday meal, Socrates, eating just enough that I am neither empty nor overfull for the rest of the day.

By Hera, Ischomachus, I said, what you do pleases me very much indeed. For to make use, at the same time, of the very same preparations both for health and strength, and for military training, and for the cultivation of wealth, all seem to me admirable practices.

And indeed you offer sufficient proof that you attend to each of these rightly: for we generally see you, with the gods' help, healthy and strong, and we know you are said to be among the most skilled at horsemanship and among the wealthiest.
Doing these things, then, Socrates, said Ischomachus, I am very much slandered by many people; but you perhaps thought I was going to say that I am called a gentleman by many.

But in fact I was about to ask this too: whether you take any trouble also over being able to give and receive an account, should you ever need to. For do you not seem to yourself, Socrates, to be continually practising this very thing -- defending yourself on the grounds that you wrong no one, but do good to as many as you can -- and do you not seem to yourself to practise accusing men too, when you observe many wronging both private individuals and the city, but doing good to no one?

But if you also practise expressing such things, this too, Ischomachus, I said, still show me. I never cease practising this, Socrates, he said. For either, hearing someone accusing or defending one of the servants, I try to test the arguments, or I find fault with or praise someone among my friends, or I reconcile some of my acquaintances, trying to teach them that it is more advantageous for them to be friends than enemies,

or we criticize some general when present together, or we defend someone if he is unjustly blamed, or we accuse one another if someone is unjustly honoured. And often too, when deliberating, we praise what we wish to do, and find fault with what we do not wish to do.

And already, Socrates, he said, I have often been judged, in a formal division of a case, as to what penalty I should suffer or pay. By whom, Ischomachus, I said? For this had escaped me. By my wife, he said. And how, I said, do you argue your case? Quite reasonably, whenever it is to my advantage to tell the truth; but when it is false, by Zeus, I cannot, Socrates, make the weaker argument the stronger.
