And I said: Perhaps, Ischomachus, it is because you cannot make the false true.

div.head: Training a steward: the master's eye fattens the horse
div.p: But look here, I said, let me not keep you from leaving, since you are already wishing to go. By Zeus, Socrates, he said, I would not leave before the marketplace has entirely broken up.

By Zeus, I said, you are indeed carefully guarding against losing your title -- being called a gentleman. For now, though perhaps many things need your attention, since you have arranged to meet the foreigners, you wait for them, so as not to break your word. But indeed, Socrates, said Ischomachus, none of what you speak of is neglected by me either; for I have overseers on my farms.

And when you need an overseer, I said, do you seek out a man skilled in overseeing and try to acquire him, just as, when you need a carpenter, I well know you look for someone skilled in carpentry and try to secure him -- or do you train your overseers yourself?

Yes, by Zeus, Socrates, said Ischomachus, I try to train them myself. For whoever is going to be capable of taking my place when I am absent -- overseeing in my stead -- what else does he need to know than what I myself know? For if I am capable of directing the work, I could surely teach another what I myself understand.

Then must he first have goodwill toward you and yours, if he is to be sufficient in your absence? For without goodwill, what use is any knowledge whatsoever in an overseer? None at all, by Zeus, said Ischomachus, and indeed I try to train goodwill toward myself and mine first of all.
And how, by the gods, do you teach whomever you wish to have goodwill toward you and yours? By doing good to them, by Zeus, said Ischomachus, whenever the gods give us some abundance of good things.
You mean, then, I said, that those who share in your good fortune become well-disposed toward you and wish you well? For this, Socrates, I find to be the best instrument of goodwill there is.

But if he does become well-disposed toward you, Ischomachus, I said, is that alone enough to make him a capable overseer? Do you not see that even men who are well-disposed toward themselves -- indeed nearly all human beings -- are nonetheless often unwilling to take the trouble to secure for themselves the good things they desire?
But by Zeus, said Ischomachus, when I wish to appoint such overseers, I teach diligence too.

How, by the gods? I said. For I thought this was entirely impossible to teach -- to make a man diligent. Indeed, Socrates, he said, it is not possible to teach absolutely everyone, one after another, in this way, to be diligent.

What sort of men, then, I said, is it possible to teach? Tell me clearly, above all, this. First, Socrates, he said, you could not make men who are slaves to drink diligent; for drunkenness causes forgetfulness of everything one needs to do.

Are those, then, I said, who are slaves to drink the only ones incapable of diligence, or are there others too? Yes, by Zeus, said Ischomachus, those who are slaves to sleep too; for neither could such a man, while asleep, do what is needed himself, nor could he set others to do it.

What then? I said. Will these be the only ones we shall find incapable of being taught this diligence, or are there others besides? It seems to me, said Ischomachus, that those hopelessly in love with sexual pleasures too are incapable of being taught to attend to anything more than that;

for it is not easy to find any hope or care sweeter than the care of one's beloved, nor, when the moment for action comes, is it easy to find any punishment more grievous than being kept from one's darling. Wherefore I hold back, and do not even attempt to appoint as overseers any I know to be of this sort.

What about those, I said, who are passionately fond of gain -- are these too incapable of being trained to take care of farm-work? Not at all, by Zeus, said Ischomachus, not in the least; indeed they are quite easily led toward such diligence; for one need only show them that diligence is profitable.

As for the rest, I said, if they are self-controlled in the things you require of them, and are moderately inclined toward gain, how do you teach them to become diligent in what you wish them to attend to? Quite simply, Socrates, said Ischomachus. For whenever I see them being diligent, I praise them and try to honour them; but whenever I see them being negligent, I try to say and do things that will sting them.

Come then, Ischomachus, I said, tell me this too, turning aside a moment from the subject of those being trained toward diligence, to the subject of training itself: is it possible for a man who is himself negligent to make others diligent?

No, by Zeus, said Ischomachus, no more than it is possible for a man who is himself unmusical to make others musicians. For it is difficult for a pupil to learn to do a thing well when the teacher demonstrates it badly, and it is difficult for a servant to become diligent when the master shows him negligence.

And to put it briefly, I do not think I have ever come to know good servants belonging to a bad master; I have, however, already seen bad servants belonging to a good one -- not unpunished, though. But the man who wishes to make some of his people diligent must be able both to oversee the work and to examine it closely, and must be willing to render thanks to the one responsible for what is well accomplished, and must not hesitate to impose the deserved penalty on the negligent.

And the response attributed to the foreigner seems well put to me too, said Ischomachus: when a king, having come into possession of a good horse and wishing to fatten it as quickly as possible, asked one of those thought skilled in horses what fattens a horse fastest, the man is said to have answered: the master's eye. So too, Socrates, he said, it seems to me the master's eye is what most produces fine and good results in everything else as well.

div.head: Teaching a steward justice
div.p: Whenever, then, I said, you have impressed upon someone, quite firmly, that he must attend diligently to whatever you wish, will such a man already be sufficiently capable of overseeing, or must he learn something more besides, if he is to be a capable overseer?

Yes, by Zeus, said Ischomachus, there still remains for him to learn what must be done, and when, and how; otherwise, what use would an overseer be, lacking these things, any more than a physician who attends to a patient early and late, but does not know what is beneficial for the patient to do?

And if indeed he also learns how the work must be done, will he still need anything further, I said, or will he already be a finished overseer for you? I think, he said, he must also learn to command those who are working.

Do you, then, I said, also train your overseers to be capable of commanding? I certainly try to, said Ischomachus. And how, by the gods, do you teach them to be capable of commanding men? Quite poorly, Socrates, he said, so that you might well laugh when you hear it.

The matter is not, however, worthy of laughter, Ischomachus, I said. For whoever is able to make men capable of commanding is clearly also able to teach them to be capable of mastering others, and whoever is able to make them capable of mastering others is also able to teach them to be capable of ruling as kings. So the man capable of doing this seems to me worthy not of laughter but of great praise.
Well, said he, Socrates, the other animals learn to obey through these two things: through being punished when they attempt to disobey, and through being well treated when they serve willingly.
Colts, at any rate, learn to obey their trainers because when they obey they get some pleasant treat, and when they disobey they have trouble, until they serve the trainer's wishes;

and puppies too, though far inferior to human beings in judgment and speech, nonetheless learn to run in circles, to tumble, and many other things, in this same way; for when they obey, they get something they want, and when they are careless, they are punished.

Human beings, however, can be made more persuadable through speech as well, by demonstrating to them that it is to their advantage to obey; but for slaves, the training that seems fit for beasts is also quite effective at teaching obedience; for by indulging their bellies according to their desires, one can accomplish much with them. And ambitious natures too are spurred on by praise; for some natures hunger for praise no less than others hunger for food and drink.

These same methods, then, which I myself use, I believe, to make men more persuadable, I teach to whomever I wish to appoint as overseers, and I assist them in this in the following ways as well: the clothing that I must provide to the workers, and the shoes, I do not make all alike, but some worse, some better, so that it may be possible to honour the better worker with the better item, and give the lesser thing to the lesser man.

For it seems to me, Socrates, he said, that despondency arises in good workers, when they see their own tasks being accomplished through their own efforts, while those unwilling to work or take risks when needed receive the same treatment as themselves.

I myself, then, do not think the better workers deserve to receive the same as the worse in any way whatsoever; and when I know that the overseers have given the best rewards to those most deserving, I praise them; but if I see anyone being favoured through flattery or some other useless act of favouritism, I do not overlook it, but rebuke them and try to teach them, Socrates, that such behaviour is not even in their own interest.

div.head: Justice and reward among the household slaves
div.p: And when, Ischomachus, I said, you have made someone sufficiently capable of commanding, so as to produce obedience, do you consider him already a finished overseer, or does the man who has all this that you have described still need something more?

Yes, by Zeus, said Ischomachus, he still needs to keep his hands off his master's property, and not steal. For if the man handling the crops should dare to make them disappear, so that no profit is left for the work, what use would there be in farming with such a man's oversight?
Do you, then, teach this kind of justice too? I do indeed, he said; but I do not find everyone readily obedient to this teaching.

Nonetheless, taking some things from the laws of Draco and others from the laws of Solon, I try to instil justice in my servants. For these men too seem to me to have established many of their laws with just this kind of teaching in mind.

For it is written that thieves should be punished, that whoever is caught in the act should be imprisoned, and that those who attempt more serious wrongs should be put to death. It is clear, then, he said, that they wrote these laws wishing to make dishonest gain unprofitable for wrongdoers.
I, then, applying some of these principles, and citing some other examples taken from royal laws as well, try to make my servants just in the handling of what is entrusted to them.

For those human laws are merely penalties for wrongdoers, but the royal laws not only punish the unjust, but also benefit the just; so that many people, seeing that the just grow wealthier than the unjust, though they are very fond of gain, hold quite firmly to not doing wrong.
But whomever I perceive still trying to do wrong, even after being well treated, these I now regard as incorrigibly grasping, and I remove them from any further use.

But whomever I find to be just not merely because gaining more makes it worthwhile, but because they also desire to be praised by me -- these I now treat as free men, not only enriching them but also honouring them as gentlemen.

For in this, Socrates, he said, the ambitious man seems to me to differ from the gain-loving man: that he is willing, for the sake of praise and honour, to labour where necessary, to take risks, and to abstain from shameful gains.

div.head: Beginning the art of farming itself
div.p: But indeed, once you have instilled in someone the desire that good things be yours, and instilled in this same person diligence to see that these things are accomplished for you, and, beyond this, given him the knowledge of how each task might be done more profitably, and beyond this made him sufficiently capable of commanding, and on top of all this he takes pleasure in showing you the fruits of the earth in as great abundance as you take pleasure in for yourself -- I shall no longer ask about this, whether such a man still needs anything more; for such a man already seems to me to be worth a great deal as an overseer. But do not, Ischomachus, I said, leave out that point which we have run over most carelessly in our discussion.

What point is that? said Ischomachus. You said, I think, that it was most important to learn how each task should be carried out to completion; for otherwise, you said, diligence itself was of no use, unless one also knew what must be done and how it must be done.

At this, Ischomachus said: Are you now bidding me, Socrates, to teach you the very art of farming itself? For this, I said, is perhaps precisely what makes those who understand it wealthy, while those who do not understand it, despite much labour, live in helplessness.

Now then, Socrates, he said, you shall hear too of the humanity of this art. For that it is at once the most beneficial, the pleasantest to practise, the finest, and the dearest to gods and men, and, on top of all this, the easiest to learn -- how is that not noble? For we call noble too all those animals which, being fine, large, and beneficial, are gentle toward human beings.

But this, Ischomachus, I said, I feel I have sufficiently learned from what you have said, as to what one must teach an overseer: for I feel I have learned both how you said to make him well-disposed toward you, and how to make him diligent, commanding, and just.

But what you said, that the man who intends to oversee farming properly must learn what must be done, and how, and when each thing must be done -- this seems to me, I said, we have rather carelessly run over in our discussion;

as if you had said that the man who intends to be able to write down what is dictated to him, and to read what is written, must know his letters. Hearing this, I would have heard that he must know his letters, but knowing this, I do not think I would know my letters any better for it.
So too now: that the man who intends to oversee farming properly must know farming, I am easily persuaded of; but knowing this, I am no more capable of knowing how one ought to farm.

But if it seemed good to me right now to farm, I think I would be like a physician who goes around visiting the sick, but knows nothing of what benefits them. So that I may not be such a man, then, I said, teach me the actual works of farming.

But indeed, Socrates, said Ischomachus, farming is not difficult to learn, unlike the other arts, which require the learner to wear himself out before he can produce work worth his keep; rather, farming is such that, seeing some things being done, and hearing about others, you would immediately understand it, so much so that you could even teach another, if you wished. I think, he said, that you yourself already know a great deal about it without realizing it.

For indeed the other craftsmen conceal, in some way, the most important points of whatever art each possesses; but among farmers, the man who plants best would be most delighted if someone were to watch him, and likewise the man who sows best; and whatever you should ask about anything well done, he would hide nothing from you as to how he did it.
So farming, Socrates, he said, seems to produce the noblest characters too in those who practise it.

Well, the preface is fine, I said, and not the kind one can hear and then turn away from asking further; so go through it for me all the more, precisely because it is so easy to learn. For it is no shame for you to teach what is easy, but it would be far more shameful for me not to know it, especially since it happens to be useful.

div.head: Knowing the nature of the land
div.p: Well then, Socrates, said he, first I want to show you this: that what those say is most intricate about farming, who discuss it most precisely in theory but practise it least, is not in fact difficult.

For they say that the man who intends to farm rightly must first know the nature of the soil. Rightly said, I said. For the man who does not know what the land is capable of bearing could not, I think, know either what he ought to sow or what he ought to plant.

Well then, said Ischomachus, this too can be learned about someone else's land, by observing what crops and trees it bears and does not bear; and once one knows this, there is no longer any use in fighting against god. For a man would not have what he needs more by sowing and planting what he himself desires, than by sowing and planting what the land itself delights to grow and nourish.

And if the land, through the idleness of its owners, does not display its own capacity, it is often possible to learn the truth about it more accurately from a neighbouring plot of land than by asking a neighbouring person.

And even when lying fallow, it still displays its own nature; for land that produces fine wild growth is capable, when cultivated, of bringing forth fine cultivated crops as well. So then, even those without much experience of farming are nonetheless able to discern the nature of the land in this way.
But this, Ischomachus, I said, I now feel I have gained sufficient confidence in, that one need not fear, out of ignorance of the nature of the land, being kept from farming.

For indeed, I said, I am reminded of the fishermen, who, though working at sea and neither stopping to watch nor walking slowly, but running past at the same time as they pass the fields, nonetheless do not hesitate to declare, when they see crops growing in the ground, which land is good and which is bad, praising the one and censuring the other. And I observe that on most points they agree with those experienced in farming about what makes good land.
From where, then, do you wish me to begin, Socrates, said he, in reminding you about farming? For I know that I shall be telling much to a man who already understands it, about how one ought to farm.

It seems to me, Ischomachus, I said, that I would first gladly learn this (for it is most fitting for a philosophical man to inquire into) how, if I wished, I might obtain the most barley and the most wheat by working the land.
Well then, you know this at least, that fallow ground must be worked in preparation for sowing? I know that, I said.
Well then, he said, should we begin ploughing the land in winter? But it would be mud then, I said. What about in summer, do you think? The ground will be hard, I said, for the yoked oxen to move.

It is likely, then, he said, that this task should be begun in spring. Yes, I said, for it is likely the land is most easily worked when turned over at that season. And the grass turned under at that time, said Ischomachus, provides manure to the land at once, but has not yet dropped seed so as to grow again.
For I think you also know this still, that if the fallow land is going to be good, it must be free of weeds and baked as much as possible by the sun. Yes indeed, I said, I think this too must be so.

And do you think these results could come about in any other way, he said, than if one turns the land over as often as possible during the summer? I know for certain, I said, that in no way would the weeds float on the surface and wither more from the heat, or the land be baked more by the sun, than if one turned it over with the yoked oxen in the middle of summer and in the middle of the day.

And if men were to make the fallow ground by digging, he said, is it not clear that they too must separate the earth from the weeds? And the weeds, I said, must be thrown on top so that they wither, and the earth turned over so that the raw part of it is baked.

div.head: Sowing, and the parable of the drones
div.p: Concerning the fallow ground, you see, Socrates, said he, how we both think alike. So it seems, I said. But concerning the season for sowing, do you know anything else, Socrates, he said, than that season for sowing which all men of former times, having made trial of it, and all men now, making trial of it, have judged to be best?

For when the autumn season comes, all men, I think, look to the god, waiting for when, having moistened the earth with rain, he will allow them to sow. And all men, I said, Ischomachus, have surely also learned, of their own accord, not to sow in dry ground, plainly having struggled through many losses, those who used to sow before being bidden to by the god.

In this, then, said Ischomachus, we all agree with one another. Yes, I said, for whatever the god teaches, in this way agreement comes about: for instance, it seems better to everyone alike to wear thick garments in winter, if they are able, and it seems best to everyone alike to keep a fire burning, if they have wood.

But in this, said Ischomachus, many already disagree, Socrates, concerning sowing -- whether the earliest sowing is best, or the middle, or the very latest. And the god, I said, does not conduct the year in a fixed manner, but makes one year best for the earliest sowing, another for the middle, another for the latest.

Which, then, said he, Socrates, do you think it better to do -- to choose one of these times for sowing, whether one sows much or little seed, or to sow beginning from the earliest right through to the latest? And I said:

It seems to me, Ischomachus, best to have a share in every kind of sowing. For I think it far better always to obtain sufficient grain, than sometimes a very great deal and sometimes not even enough. And in this too, then, said he, Socrates, you the learner agree with me the teacher, and indeed you declared your own opinion on this before I did.

Why, I said, is there some intricate art in the throwing of the seed? By all means, he said, Socrates, let us examine this too. That the seed must be thrown from the hand, you know this too, I suppose, he said. Indeed I have seen it, I said. But some men, he said, can throw evenly, others cannot. Then this too, I said, already requires practice, just as the hand of a lyre-player needs training, so that it can serve the judgment.

Quite so, he said; but what if the land is finer in some places, coarser in others? What do you mean by that? I said. Do you mean the finer as the weaker, and the coarser as the stronger? That is what I mean, he said, and I am asking you whether you would give equal seed to each kind of land, or to which one you would give more.

As for wine, I said, I think one ought to pour more water into the stronger kind, and as for a man, if he must carry some weight, I would place a heavier load upon the stronger man; and if some people must be fed, I would assign more to feed to those most capable of it. But whether weak land becomes stronger if one throws more seed onto it, just as with pack-animals, this you must teach me.

And Ischomachus, laughing, said: You are joking, Socrates. But know this well: if, having thrown the seed into the ground, you then turn it back under while the land still has much nourishment from the sky, having become green shoot from the seed, this becomes food for the land, and strength arises in it, as it were, from manure; but if you let the land nourish the seed all the way through to the crop, it is difficult for weak land to bring forth much crop right to the end. For it is difficult too for a weak sow to raise many sturdy piglets.

Are you saying, Ischomachus, I said, that less seed must be thrown onto weaker land? Yes, by Zeus, Socrates, he said, and you agree with me too, in saying that you think fewer tasks should be assigned to weaker creatures generally.

Well then, Ischomachus, I said, for what purpose do you throw in the hoers among the grain? You know, I suppose, he said, that much water falls in winter. Why, of course, I said. Let us suppose, then, that some of the grain is buried by mud that has washed over it, and some roots are exposed by the flow of water. And weeds too, often, growing up along with the grain because of the rains, choke it. All this, I said, is likely to happen.

Do you not think, then, he said, that the grain now needs some help? Very much so, I said. Then what, in your opinion, should be done to help the grain that has been buried in mud? Lighten the soil over it, I said. And what about the grain whose roots have been laid bare? Heap the earth back around it, I said.

But what, he said, if weeds grow up and choke the grain, stealing away its nourishment, just as drones, being useless, steal the food from the bees, which the bees have worked to store up? Yes, by Zeus, one must cut away the weeds, I said, just as one removes the drones from the hives.

Do we not seem to you, then, he said, to have good reason for throwing in the hoers? Very much so. And I am struck, Ischomachus, I said, at what it is to introduce comparisons well; for you have made me quite angry at the weeds by speaking of drones, far more than when you spoke of the weeds themselves.

div.head: Reaping and threshing
div.p: And then, I said, after this, it is likely one must reap. So teach me, if you have anything to say about this too. If you do not turn out, he said, to know as much as I do about this too. Well, you know that the grain must be cut. Why should I not? I said. Would you, then, he said, stand to cut where the wind blows, or against it? Not against it, I said; for I think it is hard both on the eyes and on the hands to reap facing into the chaff and the beards of the grain.

And would you cut at the top of the stalk, he said, or close to the ground? If the stalk of the grain is short, I said, I would cut low down, so that the straw might be more useful; but if it is tall, I think it right to cut in the middle, so that neither the threshers labour needlessly, nor the winnowers need trouble themselves with what they have no use for. And what is left in the ground, I think, if burned, benefits the land, and if thrown into the manure, adds to the bulk of the manure.

You see, Socrates, said Ischomachus, how you are caught in the act, knowing about reaping too, just as I do. I run the risk of it, I said, and I want to examine whether I also know how to thresh. Well then, he said, you know this at least, that grain is threshed with the help of a yoked animal.

Why should I not know it? I said. And I know too that all such animals are called yoked animals alike, oxen, mules, horses. So do you think, he said, that these animals know only this much, to trample the grain as they are driven?

But how the necessary part is broken off and the threshing evened out, by what means is this done, Socrates? he said. Clearly, I said, by the threshers; for turning it over and continually throwing the untrodden part under their feet, they would obviously make the threshing most even and finish the work quickest. In this, then, he said, you lack nothing of what I know.

Well then, Ischomachus, I said, after this we shall clean the grain by winnowing. And tell me, Socrates, do you know that if you begin from the windward part of the threshing-floor, the chaff will be carried across the whole floor? Necessarily, I said. And it is likely, he said, that it falls upon the grain too. Indeed, I said, it is a great distance for the chaff to be carried over the grain into the empty part of the floor. And what if one winnows beginning from the leeward part? he said. Clearly, I said, it will at once be in the chaff-receptacle.

And when you have cleaned the grain halfway across the threshing-floor, he said, will you at once, with the grain still spread out this way, winnow the remaining chaff, or will you push the clean grain toward the pole, into as small a space as possible? I would push the clean grain together, by Zeus, I said, so that the chaff might be carried across to the empty part of the floor, and I would not have to winnow the same chaff twice.

So you, Socrates, he said, would already be able to teach another too how the grain might most quickly be made clean. This, then, I said, had escaped my own notice, that I knew it. And I have long been considering whether I have also, without noticing, escaped my own knowledge of goldsmithing, flute-playing, and painting; for no one taught me these things either, any more than farming -- yet I observe people practising the other arts, just as I observe them farming.

Did I not tell you long ago, said Ischomachus, that farming is also the noblest of the arts in this respect, that it is the easiest to learn? Well then, Ischomachus, I said, I know it: after all this, sowing follows next.
Well then, that too I found I already knew about the sowing of grain, it seems.

div.head: Planting trees and vines
div.p: Is the planting of trees also part of the art of farming? he said. It is indeed, said Ischomachus. Then how, I said, could I understand the matters concerning sowing, but not understand the matters concerning planting?

Do you not understand it, said Ischomachus? How could I, I said, who knows neither in what kind of soil one ought to plant, nor how deep the hole should be dug for the plant, nor how wide, nor how long the plant should be set into the ground, nor how the plant, once laid in the ground, would sprout best?

Come then, said Ischomachus, learn what you do not know. You have surely seen, I suppose, the pits they dig for plants. And often, I said. Have you then ever seen one deeper than three feet? Not even, by Zeus, I said, one two and a half feet deep. And what about the width -- have you ever seen one wider than three feet? Not even, by Zeus, two feet wide, I said.

Come then, he said, answer me this too: have you ever seen one shallower than one foot in depth? Not even, by Zeus, I said, one and a half feet deep. For the plants would be dug up again if they were planted too shallow, in such a way.

This, then, Socrates, you already know sufficiently, that they dig neither deeper than two and a half feet nor shallower than one and a half feet. Necessarily, I said, this must be so, being so plainly visible. And what about this, he said, do you know how to distinguish drier from moister land by sight? Dry, at least, seems to me to be the land around Lycabettus and land like it, and moist the land in the Phaleric marsh and land like it.

And do you know, he said, how to recognize drier and moister land by sight? Dry, at least, seems to me, I said, to be the land around Lycabettus and land like it, and moist the land in the Phaleric marsh and land like it.

Would you, then, he said, dig a deep hole for the plant in the dry land or the moist land? In the dry land, by Zeus, I said; since if you dig deep in moist land, you would find water, and could no longer plant in water. You seem to me to speak well, he said. Now once the pits are dug, have you seen when it is time to set each kind of plant into them?

Very much so, I said. Now you, wishing them to sprout as quickly as possible, do you think that by placing them beneath worked soil, the shoot of the cutting would pass more quickly through soft ground, or through untilled hard ground? Clearly, I said, it would sprout faster through worked soil than through untilled ground.

Then soil must be placed beneath the plant. What else could it be, I said. And do you think that setting the whole cutting upright, looking toward the sky, it would take root better, or would you set some part of it at an angle beneath the soil, so that it lies like an inverted gamma?

That way, by Zeus; for there would be more buds beneath the earth; and I see the plants sprout upward from the buds. And I think the buds beneath the earth do this same thing. And with many shoots growing beneath the earth, I think the plant would sprout quickly and strongly.

In this too, then, he said, you happen to think exactly as I do. Would you merely heap the soil around, or would you also pack it firmly around the plant? I would pack it firmly, by Zeus, I said; for if it were not packed down, I know well that the unpacked soil would become mud from the rain, and dry all the way through from the sun, so that there is a danger the plants would rot from the moisture, or wither from the dryness, if the roots became overheated because the earth is too loose.

So concerning the planting of vines too, Socrates, he said, you happen to know all the same things as I do. And should we plant a fig tree the same way? he said. I think, said Ischomachus, all the other fruit-bearing trees too. For what would you reject, from what is done well in planting the vine, when it comes to planting other trees?

But how shall we plant the olive tree, Ischomachus? I said. You are testing me on this too, though you know it best of all yourself. You see, of course, that a deeper hole is dug for the olive; for it is dug especially deep along the roads too; and you see that stumps are set with all the cuttings; and you see, he said, that clay is placed on top of the heads of all the plants, and the top of every plant is covered.

I see all this, I said. And seeing it, then, he said, what is it that you do not understand? Or do you not know, Socrates, he said, how one should set the potsherd on top of the clay? By Zeus, I said, none of what you have described is unknown to me, Ischomachus, but I am wondering again just why, when a while ago you asked me flatly whether I knew how to plant, I said I did not. For I did not think I would be able to say anything about how one ought to plant; but since you undertook to question me point by point, I answer you, as you yourself say, exactly what you, the man called a clever farmer, know.

Is questioning, then, Ischomachus, I said, a form of teaching? For I have just now come to understand the way you were questioning me about each thing. Leading me through what I knew, and pointing out things similar to what I did not think I knew, you persuade me, I think, that I know these things too.

Then, said Ischomachus, if I were to question you about money too, whether it is good or not, could I persuade you that you know how to distinguish good coin from counterfeit coin? Could I persuade you, questioning about flute-players, that you know how to play the flute, and about painters and other such craftsmen? Perhaps, I said, since you have also persuaded me that I understand farming, though I know full well that no one has ever taught me this art.
That is not so, Socrates, he said; but I told you long ago that farming is such a humane and gentle art that merely by seeing and hearing it, it makes people knowledgeable in it at once.

And it teaches much itself, he said, as to how one might best make use of it. The vine, for instance, climbing up a nearby tree when it has one close by, teaches you to prop it up; and spreading out its leaves while the clusters are still tender, it teaches you to shade what is exposed to the sun at that season;

and when the time comes for the grapes to be sweetened by the sun, by shedding its leaves it teaches itself how to bare and ripen its fruit; and, through its abundant bearing, by showing some clusters ripe while carrying others still unripe, it teaches you to harvest it in the way one harvests figs, taking always what is ready.

div.head: Why some farmers prosper and others fail: diligence over knowledge
div.p: At this point, I said: How is it, then, Ischomachus, if the matters concerning farming are indeed so easy to learn, and everyone knows equally what must be done, that not everyone fares equally well, but some of them live in abundance and have a surplus, while others cannot even provide themselves with what is necessary, but even fall into debt?
I will tell you, Socrates, said Ischomachus. It is not knowledge or ignorance on the part of the farmers that makes some prosper and others fall into difficulty;

nor would you hear the story going about that a household has been ruined because the sower did not sow evenly, or because he did not plant the rows straight, or because someone, not knowing what kind of land bears vines, planted them in unproductive soil, or because someone did not know it is good to work the fallow ground before sowing, or because someone did not know it is good to mix manure into the soil;

but rather one is far more likely to hear it said: the man does not get grain from his field, because he takes no care that it be sown, or that manure be provided for it. Nor does the man have wine, because he takes no care to plant vines, nor that the ones he has bear fruit for him. Nor does the man have oil or figs, because he takes no care and does nothing to see that he has these.

These, Socrates, are the things in which farmers differ from one another, and by which they act so very differently -- far more than by any clever discovery they have supposedly made concerning the actual work.

And even generals, in some cases, are better or worse than one another at the work of generalship, not through any difference in judgment, but clearly through diligence. For what both the generals and most private soldiers alike know, some commanders do, others do not.

For instance, everyone knows that when marching through hostile territory, it is better to march in the formation best suited for fighting, should the need arise. Knowing this, however, some do it this way, others do not.
Everyone knows that it is better to post guards, both by day and by night, in front of the camp. But even of this, some take care that it be so, others do not take care.

And again, when passing through narrow places, it is not at all difficult to find someone who does not know it is better to seize the key positions beforehand than not to. But even of this, some take care to do so, others do not.

And likewise, everyone says that manure is best for farming, and they see it being produced naturally; yet, though it is a simple matter to know how it comes about, and easy to produce a great quantity of it, some take care that it be gathered, while others neglect this entirely.

And yet the god above provides the water, and every hollow place becomes a marsh, and the earth produces every kind of weed, and the man who intends to sow must clear the land; and whatever is cleared away and thrown into the water, time itself will turn into what the land delights in. For what kind of weeds, or what kind of soil, does not turn into manure when left standing in water?

And as for whatever treatment the land needs -- whether it is too wet for sowing, or too salty for planting -- these too everyone knows, both that the water is drained off by ditches, and that the salt is corrected by mixing in fresh, unsalted matter, both wet and dry; but of this too, some take care, and others do not.

And if a man were altogether ignorant of what the earth is able to produce, and had no crop or plant of its own to see, nor anyone to hear the truth about it from, is it not much easier for every man to make trial of the land than of a horse, and much easier still than of a man? For the land shows nothing for the sake of deception, but plainly and truthfully reveals what it can and cannot do.

It seems to me that the land examines and reveals the bad and lazy men most clearly of all, by making everything so knowable and easy to learn. For unlike the other arts, where those who do not work can make excuses that they do not understand them, everyone knows that the land, treated well, treats well in return;

so that idleness applied to the land is a clear accusation of a wicked soul. For no one persuades himself that he can live without the necessities of life; and the man who neither knows another money-making art nor is willing to farm is clearly planning to live by stealing, robbing, or begging -- or else he is altogether without reason.

It makes a great difference too, he said, in whether farming is profitable or not, when, there being several hired labourers, one man takes some care that the workers be on the job at the right time, and another does not take this care. For one man alone, working in due season, easily makes a difference equal to ten who do not, and another man too makes a difference simply by leaving off before the proper time.
And letting men slack off idly through the whole day easily makes a difference of half the entire work.

Just as on journeys, sometimes men differ from one another in speed by as much as a hundred stades over a distance of two hundred, though both are young and healthy -- when the one does what he has set out to do, walking steadily, while the other takes it easy in his mind, resting by springs and in the shade, looking about, and chasing after gentle breezes.

So too in their work, there is a great difference in accomplishment between those who do what they are set to do, and those who do not do it, but find excuses for not working and are allowed to idle away their time.

And this matter of working well or working badly makes as great a difference as that between working at all and not working at all. For instance, when men dig around the vines to clear them of weeds, if they dig in such a way that the weeds grow back thicker and finer, how could you not call this idleness in disguise?

These things, then, are what ruin households far more than any excessive ignorance. For when expenses run out fully from a household, while the work does not turn out profitably in proportion to the expense, one need no longer be surprised if, instead of a surplus, want results.

But for those capable of taking care and farming with real diligence, my own father too practised, and taught me, the most effective way of making money from farming. For he never allowed me to buy land that had already been worked, but urged me to buy any that was idle and unplanted, either through the negligence or the incapacity of its owners.

For, he said, worked land fetches a great price and admits of no further improvement; but land not improved, he considered, offers no similar pleasure either -- rather, he thought that every possession and every creature that is improving gives the greatest delight. And nothing offers greater improvement than land brought from being idle to being fully productive.

For know well, Socrates, he said, that we have already made many plots of land worth many times their original price. And this idea, Socrates, is worth so much, and so easy to learn, that now, having heard it from me, you go away knowing it as well as I do, and could teach it to another, if you wished.

And my father neither learned this from another nor discovered it through careful thought, but said that, out of his love for farming and hard work, he desired such land, that he might have something to occupy him while also taking pleasure in the benefit he gained.

For my father, Socrates, he said, was by nature, it seems to me, the most devoted farmer among the Athenians. And hearing this, I asked him: But did your father keep all the plots of land he improved, Ischomachus, or did he also sell them, if he found a good price for them? He did sell them, by Zeus, said Ischomachus; but he would immediately buy another one in its place, an idle one, because of his love of work.

You are saying, Ischomachus, I said, that your father was truly by nature as fond of farming as merchants are fond of grain. For merchants too, out of their great love for grain, sail wherever they hear there is the most of it, crossing the Aegean, the Black Sea, and the Sicilian sea to get it;

and then, having taken as much as they can, they carry it across the sea, loading it onto the very ship they themselves sail in. And when they need money, they do not throw it away carelessly, wherever they happen to be, but carry it to wherever they hear grain is valued most highly and people esteem it most, and deliver it to them there. Your father too seems to have been a lover of farming in much the same way.

To this Ischomachus said: You are joking, Socrates; but I consider men equally fond of building who sell the houses they build, and then build others. By Zeus, I said, and I swear to you, Ischomachus, that I truly believe you, that it is natural for all men to love whatever they believe brings them benefit.

div.head: The gift of command
div.p: But indeed, I said, Ischomachus, I am reflecting on how well you have supported your whole argument by your original thesis; for you proposed that the art of farming is the easiest of all to learn, and now, from everything you have said, I am entirely persuaded by you that this is so.

Yes, by Zeus, said Ischomachus, but as for this, Socrates -- that quality common to all pursuits alike, to farming, to statecraft, to household management, and to warfare -- the capacity to command -- in this, I agree with you, men differ greatly from one another in judgment;

just as on a trireme, he said, when out at sea and needing to make a day's voyage by rowing, some boatswains are able to speak and act in such a way as to sharpen the spirits of the men so that they work willingly, while others are so lacking in judgment that they take more than twice as long to complete the same voyage. And the one group disembark having sweated and praised one another, the boatswain and the crew alike, while the others arrive without having sweated at all, hating their overseer and being hated by him in turn.

And generals differ from one another in just this respect: some produce men neither willing to work nor to face danger, unwilling even to obey except under compulsion, but even priding themselves on opposing their commander; while these same men, under other generals, do not even know how to be ashamed, should anything shameful occur.

But truly divine and good and knowledgeable commanders, taking charge of these very same men, and often others besides, find them ashamed to do anything shameful, and believing it better to obey, taking pride, each man and all together, in obeying, and, when there is need, working without discouragement.

And just as with private individuals a certain love of labour sometimes arises, so too, under good commanders, love of labour and ambition to be seen doing something fine by the commander arise in the whole army.

And toward whatever commander the followers are so disposed, these become truly vigorous commanders -- not, by Zeus, those who are physically the best of the soldiers, throw the javelin best, shoot the bow best, or, having the finest horse, take the lead in danger as the finest horseman or the finest peltast -- but those who can instil in their soldiers the willingness to follow through fire and every danger.

These men one might justly call great-minded, whom many follow, knowing this to be their character; and rightly might one be said to march with a mighty force, whose judgment many hands are willing to serve; and truly great is that man who can accomplish great things by judgment rather than by physical strength.

So too in private undertakings, whether the man set over the work is a steward or an overseer, whoever is able to make the workers eager, diligent, and steady at their tasks -- this is the man who accomplishes good results and creates great surplus.

And when the master appears among the workers, Socrates, he said, if that master, without the workers showing any outward sign, is able to greatly harm the bad worker and greatly honour the diligent one, I would not admire him much; but if, when the workers see him, they are stirred, and vigour falls upon each of the workers, and rivalry with one another, and ambition to excel each other arises -- this man, I would say, has something of a kingly character about him.

And this seems to me the greatest thing, in every work in which anything is accomplished through human beings -- and in farming too. I do not say, however, that this can be learned merely by seeing it once, or by hearing it once; rather, I say that the man who is going to be capable of this needs education, and must have a good nature to begin with, and, most important of all, must become something divine.

For this good does not seem to me to be entirely human, but divine -- the power to make men willing to obey; which is clearly granted to those truly perfected in self-control; but the power to rule the unwilling is granted, it seems to me, to those the gods judge worthy to live as Tantalus is said to spend all his time in Hades, in fear of dying a second death.
